cards.front: Word order · not only … but also
cards.meaning: The pair gives extra emphasis to two related points.
cards.example: Ladi is gifted not only in music but also in maths.
cards.trap: Placing only not before the first point.

rule.text: Put not only before the first parallel part and but also before the second.
rule.right: Ladi sings not only at school but also at church.
rule.wrong: Ladi sings only not at school but also at church.

cards.meaning: An indirect yes/no question starts with a linking word.
cards.example: The teacher asked if we had seen the notice.
cards.trap: Leaving the question in direct form after asked.

rule.text: Use if or whether and put the subject before the verb.
rule.right: The driver asked if I had paid.
rule.wrong: The driver asked did I pay.

cards.meaning: More can change the degree of the adjective that comes next.
cards.example: The market needs more reliable evening transport.
cards.trap: Separating more from the adjective it modifies.

rule.text: Keep more next to the adjective it modifies.
rule.right: The market needs more reliable evening transport.
rule.wrong: The market needs reliable more evening transport.

cards.meaning: A final apostrophe can show that several people own something.
cards.example: The prefect collected the girls' bags before assembly.
cards.trap: Adding another s after an already plural ending.

rule.text: For a regular plural ending in s, add an apostrophe after that s.
rule.right: The girls' bags were in the hall.
rule.wrong: The girls's bags were in the hall.

cards.meaning: Information names material that English usually treats as an amount.
cards.example: The school sends information by text message.
cards.trap: Adding a plural s to information.

rule.text: Use singular verb agreement with information and count pieces of it if needed.
rule.right: The information is on the noticeboard.
rule.wrong: The informations are on the noticeboard.

cards.meaning: One person or thing is selected from a larger group.
cards.example: Ada is one of the fastest runners in Kano.
cards.trap: Putting a singular noun after one of.

rule.text: Use a plural noun for the group after one of.
rule.right: Ada is one of the school runners.
rule.wrong: Ada is one of the school runner.

cards.meaning: Some verbs keep the same form in the simple past.
cards.example: The danfo tyre burst near the market.
cards.trap: Adding ed to burst.

rule.text: Use burst for the simple past of burst.
rule.right: The balloon burst at assembly.
rule.wrong: The balloon bursted at assembly.

cards.front: Tense · used to for a past habit
cards.meaning: Used to describes a repeated action that no longer happens.
cards.example: Musa used to walk to school before he moved.
cards.trap: Dropping the d in a positive sentence.

rule.text: Use used to plus the base verb in positive statements about past habits.
rule.right: We used to walk to school.
rule.wrong: We use to walk to school.

cards.meaning: In a reported wh-question, the words after the question word follow statement order.
cards.example: Ada asked where the clinic was.
cards.trap: Putting the verb before the subject in the reported clause.

rule.text: After the wh-word, put the subject before the verb.
rule.right: Ada asked where the clinic was.
rule.wrong: Ada asked where was the clinic.

cards.meaning: Adjectives that describe material sit close to the noun.
cards.example: The stall sold black leather belts.
cards.trap: Putting the material before the colour.

rule.text: When both adjectives precede a noun, colour normally comes before material.
rule.right: The stall sold black leather belts.
rule.wrong: The stall sold leather black belts.

cards.meaning: A tag for a positive simple-past clause usually checks agreement with didn't.
cards.example: The pupils left at noon, didn't they?
cards.trap: Using isn't it as a tag for a past action.

rule.text: Use didn't plus the matching subject pronoun after a positive simple-past clause with an ordinary verb.
rule.right: The pupils left at noon, didn't they?
rule.wrong: The pupils left at noon, isn't it?

cards.meaning: A present form can move back into the past when the reporting verb is past.
cards.example: Amina asked what the assembly rules were.
cards.trap: Keeping are in an indirect question about rules that no longer apply.

rule.text: Use were when backshifting are in past reporting.
rule.right: Amina asked what the former rules were.
rule.wrong: Amina asked what the former rules are.

cards.meaning: Theirs stands on its own in place of a noun phrase showing ownership.
cards.example: Our stall is near the road and theirs is by the gate.
cards.trap: Writing their's as if it needed an apostrophe.

rule.text: Write the independent possessive pronoun theirs with no apostrophe.
rule.right: The smaller stall is theirs.
rule.wrong: The smaller stall is their's.

cards.front: Word order · neither in short replies
cards.meaning: Neither can show that a negative statement also applies to you.
cards.example: “I haven't paid the fare.” “Neither have I.”
cards.trap: Keeping normal subject–verb order after neither in a short reply.

rule.text: Use neither plus the matching auxiliary and then the subject.
rule.right: “I haven't paid the fare.” “Neither have I.”
rule.wrong: “I haven't paid the fare.” “Neither I have.”

cards.meaning: This pattern imagines a different past result.
cards.example: If Chidi had trained harder, he would have won in Enugu.
cards.trap: Using simple past alone for the if-clause about an unreal past.

rule.text: Use if plus had and a past participle, then would have plus a past participle in the result.
rule.right: If Chidi had trained harder, he would have won.
rule.wrong: If Chidi trained harder, he would have won.

cards.meaning: Whoever can mean any person who does something.
cards.example: Give the ticket to whoever asks for it first at the park.
cards.trap: Choosing whomever because of the previous preposition when the pronoun begins a clause as its subject.

rule.text: Use whoever as the subject of its own clause.
rule.right: Give the ticket to whoever asks first.
rule.wrong: Give the ticket to whomever asks first.

cards.meaning: This form looks back at an ongoing action from another past point.
cards.example: The team had been training for an hour when the rain started.
cards.trap: Using has been with a past reference point.

rule.text: Use had been and the -ing form for a continuing action before a point in the past.
rule.right: They had been training when the rain started.
rule.wrong: They has been training when the rain started.

cards.meaning: Have agrees with plural subjects in this present-perfect pattern.
cards.example: The uniforms have been washed for assembly.
cards.trap: Using has with a plural subject.

rule.text: Use have been, followed by the past participle, with plural subjects in this present-perfect passive.
rule.right: The uniforms have been washed.
rule.wrong: The uniforms has been washed.

cards.front: Tense · a finished time with ago
cards.meaning: Ago places a completed event a given distance back from now.
cards.example: The Kano bus left two hours ago.
cards.trap: Using the present perfect with a finished time introduced by ago.

rule.text: Use the simple past for a completed event dated with ago.
rule.right: The Kano bus left two hours ago.
rule.wrong: The Kano bus has left two hours ago.

cards.meaning: Were is the ordinary past form of be with a plural subject.
cards.example: The mechanic said the danfo brakes were worn.
cards.trap: Using was for plural subjects such as brakes.

rule.text: Use were with an ordinary plural subject in the past tense.
rule.right: The brakes were worn.
rule.wrong: The brakes was worn.

cards.meaning: Had can begin a formal conditional clause in place of if.
cards.example: Had Ada left earlier, she would have caught the bus to Jos.
cards.trap: Keeping the subject before had after dropping if.

rule.text: When if is omitted in this construction, put had before the subject.
rule.right: Had Ada left earlier, she would have caught the bus.
rule.wrong: Ada had left earlier, she would have caught the bus.

cards.meaning: A tag after a positive was clause usually has a negative form of be.
cards.example: Bola was at assembly, wasn't she?
cards.trap: Using didn't in a tag when the main verb is was.

rule.text: Copy the form of be and switch a positive clause to a negative tag.
rule.right: Bola was at assembly, wasn't she?
rule.wrong: Bola was at assembly, didn't she?

cards.meaning: A negative statement normally takes a positive tag.
cards.example: Amina doesn't trade on Sundays, does she?
cards.trap: Repeating the negative in the tag of a neutral confirmation question.

rule.text: After doesn't, use the positive tag does plus the subject pronoun.
rule.right: Amina doesn't trade on Sundays, does she?
rule.wrong: Amina doesn't trade on Sundays, doesn't she?

cards.meaning: Material names such as sand and cement usually refer to quantities.
cards.example: The builder mixed sand and cement behind the classroom.
cards.trap: Putting a directly before an uncountable material noun.

rule.text: Use a measure such as a bag of when counting a material like cement.
rule.right: The workers bought cement.
rule.wrong: The workers bought a cement.

cards.front: Tense · past perfect for the earlier event
cards.meaning: The past perfect can make it clear which of two past events came first.
cards.example: Before the lesson, Tayo had believed all seeds grew at the same speed.
cards.trap: Using a present form for a belief that changed before now.

rule.text: To mark an earlier state against a past reference, use had plus the past participle.
rule.right: Before the lesson, Tayo had believed that rumour.
rule.wrong: Before the lesson yesterday, Tayo has believed that rumour.

cards.meaning: For introduces a duration and since introduces a starting point.
cards.example: The pupils have been waiting at the bus park for ten minutes.
cards.trap: Using since before a length of time.

rule.text: Use for with an amount of time and since with a starting date or time.
rule.right: The pupils have waited for ten minutes.
rule.wrong: The pupils have waited since ten minutes.

cards.front: Pronouns and determiners · any after a negative
cards.meaning: Any can express an unrestricted amount after a negative verb.
cards.example: The treasurer didn't have any change for the bus fare.
cards.trap: Adding a second negative with no in standard classroom English.

rule.text: Use any after a negative verb to express a single negative.
rule.right: I didn't have any change.
rule.wrong: I didn't have no change.

cards.front: Concord · subject with a contrasting phrase
cards.meaning: A phrase giving a contrast does not replace the actual subject.
cards.example: The coach, not the players, was responsible for the school kit.
cards.trap: Making the verb agree with the nearby plural noun players.

rule.text: Match the verb to the main subject, ignoring a separate not phrase.
rule.right: The coach, not the players, was responsible.
rule.wrong: The coach, not the players, were responsible.

cards.meaning: In British English, a positive ought to clause can take an oughtn’t tag.
cards.example: We ought to thank the referee, oughtn’t we?
cards.trap: Using a tag with an unrelated form such as isn’t it.

rule.text: When repeating ought in the tag, use oughtn’t plus the subject pronoun.
rule.right: We ought to thank the referee, oughtn’t we?
rule.wrong: We ought to thank the referee, isn’t it?

cards.front: Concord · one person with two titles
cards.meaning: Two titles can refer to the same person and take a singular verb.
cards.example: The club's coach and treasurer is Amina.
cards.trap: Making the verb plural even though both titles belong to one person.

rule.text: When two titles name a single person, use a singular verb.
rule.right: Amina, our coach and treasurer, is here.
rule.wrong: Amina, our coach and treasurer, are here.
